title: Quick Draw Bandits: Quickly Optimizing in Nonstationary Environments with Extremely Many Arms

problem.claim: Multi-armed bandit methods must optimize rewards when the environment may be nonstationary and the action space may contain extremely many arms.

gap.claim: Existing methods generally handle either nonstationarity with few arms or many arms under stationary and reward-function constraints, but not both settings together.

contributions.claim: A policy is proposed for learning reward environments over a continuous space using Gaussian interpolation.
The method efficiently learns continuous Lipschitz reward functions with O*(sqrt(T)) cumulative regret.
The policy is extended to nonstationary problems through a simple modification.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe the proposed policy as novel.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The method is reported to be computationally favorable, running 100–10000 times faster than the compared sliding Gaussian process policies.
The method is reported to experimentally outperform sliding Gaussian process policies on datasets with nonstationarity and an extremely large number of arms.

narrative_sequence.summary: Canonical bandit algorithms typically assume stationary rewards and a small action space.
Recent methods usually relax only one of these assumptions, leaving a gap for settings combining nonstationarity with many arms.
The manuscript proposes a Gaussian-interpolation policy for learning reward environments over a continuous space.
The method is analyzed for regret, extended to nonstationary problems, and evaluated for computational speed and performance against sliding Gaussian process policies.

source_observation.claim: A continuous-space policy based on Gaussian interpolation is reported to address environments with many arms and can be modified for nonstationarity.

interpretation.claim: A unified modeling approach may help address multiple bandit difficulties when the action space is large and rewards change over time.

application.claim: For optimization over large or continuous action spaces with changing rewards, consider interpolation-based policies with explicit nonstationary adaptations.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish performance beyond the stated continuous Lipschitz setting or the reported datasets.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the precise algorithm, assumptions, or proof details behind the regret bound.
The abstract does not describe the datasets, baselines, experimental protocol, or statistical uncertainty.
The abstract does not quantify the nonstationary extension's regret or computational guarantees.
